issues.legal_issue: The Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes about whether listed property is wakf property and whether a listed wakf is Shia or Sunni, but that exclusion does not extend to other disputes merely because they concern wakf property.
material_facts: The properties in the eviction suits were admitted to be wakf properties.
The disputes concerned eviction of tenants, not whether the properties were wakf property or whether the wakf was Shia or Sunni.
issues.conclusion: The statutory exclusion of civil-court jurisdiction under Sections 6 and 7 is confined to the questions those provisions specify and does not cover tenant-eviction disputes.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 6(1), 6(5) and 7 of the Wakf Act, 1995 assign the Tribunal disputes about whether listed property is wakf property and whether a listed wakf is Shia or Sunni, and bar civil proceedings concerning those questions. The exclusion is limited to those specified questions. The Court relied on Board of Muslim Wakfs Rajasthan v. Radha Kishan and Punjab Wakf Board v. Gram Panchayat Alias Gram Sabha in discussing the scope of Section 6.

predicates.proceeding_is_wakf_status_or_sect_disput: The proceeding concerns whether property listed as wakf property is wakf property or whether a listed wakf is Shia or Sunni.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns the status of listed property as wakf property or the sect of a listed wakf, the Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: Civil-court jurisdiction is excluded for a dispute relating to a wakf only when the governing statutory scheme requires the Tribunal to determine that dispute.
material_facts: The eviction suits concerned property admitted to be wakf property.
The Act did not provide for Tribunal proceedings to determine the eviction dispute or the lessor-lessee rights and obligations at issue.
issues.conclusion: Section 85 excludes civil-court jurisdiction only for matters the Act requires the Tribunal to determine; it does not exclude jurisdiction over the eviction suits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 85 of the Wakf Act, 1995 bars civil proceedings in respect of matters relating to a wakf or wakf property that are required by or under the Act to be determined by a Tribunal. The general presumption is that civil courts have jurisdiction over civil disputes and that its exclusion is not readily inferred; the party asserting exclusion bears the onus. The Court relied on Rajasthan SRTC v. Bal Mukund Bairwa, Pabbojan Tea Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner, Ramesh Chand Ardawatiya v. Anil Panjwani, Dhulabhai v. State of M.P., Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, State of A.P. v. Manjeti Laxmi Kantha Rao, Dhruv Green Field Ltd. v. Hukam Singh, Dwarka Prasad Agarwal v. Ramesh Chandra Agarwala, and State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam.

predicates.proceeding_is_civil_suit_about_wakf_matt: A party has brought a civil suit concerning a wakf, wakf property, or another related matter.
predicates.matter_assigned_to_tribunal: The governing statutory scheme requires the Tribunal to determine the matter in dispute.

issues.definition: Civil-court jurisdiction is excluded when a civil suit concerns a wakf-related matter that the statutory scheme requires the Tribunal to determine.

issues.legal_issue: The provision establishing the Tribunal does not itself exclude civil-court jurisdiction over a tenant-eviction dispute concerning wakf property.
material_facts: The Wakf Board brought suits before the Tribunal seeking eviction of tenants from properties admitted to be wakf properties.
The Act contained no Tribunal procedure for determining eviction of tenants from wakf property or the rights and obligations of its lessor and lessees.
The Tribunal decreed the eviction suits, and the High Court upheld those orders.
issues.conclusion: The Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to decide the eviction suits; the suits could be brought only in a competent civil court, and the Tribunal and High Court orders were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 83 of the Wakf Act, 1995 concerns the constitution, procedure, and powers of Tribunals and does not independently oust civil-court jurisdiction. Read with Sections 6, 7, and 85, the Tribunal may decide only matters assigned to it by the Act or rules. Since no such assignment covered tenant eviction or lessor-lessee rights, the civil court retained jurisdiction. The Court affirmed the approach of the Allahabad, Karnataka, Madras, and Bombay High Courts and rejected the contrary approach of the Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, and Punjab and Haryana High Courts.

predicates.proceeding_is_tenant_eviction_suit: A wakf landlord brings a suit seeking to evict a tenant occupying wakf property.
predicates.property_is_admitted_wakf_property: The parties do not dispute that the property from which eviction is sought is wakf property.
predicates.act_provides_no_tribunal_eviction_procee: The governing statutory scheme provides no Tribunal proceeding to determine the eviction dispute or the lessor-lessee rights and obligations at issue.

issues.definition: When a wakf landlord seeks to evict a tenant from property admitted to be wakf property and the statutory scheme provides no Tribunal proceeding for that dispute, the eviction suit belongs in a civil court.
